newsitem.title: GERMANY: German conference says EMU tough but possible.
newsitem.headline: German conference says EMU tough but possible.

text.p: U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs and a number of leading voices in the debate on European monetary union on Thursday painted a picture of a single European currency that was still possible, if prone to risks.

Goldman Sachs, which was hosting a conference in Frankfurt on German and EMU themes in Frankfurt, confirmed its view that a 1999 start to the single European currency was still on balance the most likely outcome.

But its optimism was tempered by caution from other speakers, from German central bank chief Hans Tietmeyer to former European Commission head Jacques Delors, that monetary union was still under threat from inner tensions caused by the project, together with economic and currency market dangers.
"We do think that the most likely event is that a start date of 1999 does get met," Gavyn Davies, chief international economist for Goldman Sachs International told the conference.
He said that such a forecast was based on the assumption that seven to eight countries would be able to participate in the first round of monetary union scheduled for 1999.

Davies added however that such a scenario was "very, very dependent on the growth rate in gross domestic product" in the major European countries, noting that even a slight deviation from currently-forecast rates could make a delay unavoidable.

Goldman Sachs is forecasting 1997 GDP growth of around 2.25 percent for both Germany and France. "If the figures come in any lower than that, we shall have a significant problem in getting anywhere near the Maastricht criteria (for EMU entry)," Davies said.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer had earlier warned that even if EMU went ahead as planned, its success was threatened by the fact that it brought under one roof countries with very different social and economic systems.

"The potential for conflicting forces -- particularly during economic and structural upheavals -- is far greater in a currency union embracing a number of member states than at the national level," he warned.

Tietmeyer urged that as a result it was important that right from the start the EMU participants were in a position to show "a high degree of internal flexibility in their markets and a common culture of stability".
"Thus lasting consolidation (in the area of state finances)...is the order of the day," he noted.

Jacques Delors, former head of the European Commission, said there was a need for a special protocol committing countries heading towards European currency union to cooperate on macro-economic policy.
He added that such any measure should not be feared as compromising the independence of a future European Central Bank, an issue that has caused apparent conflict among some European Union countries.

"The extent of cooperation has recently not been very encouraging. This is all the more reason to detail within a protocol the procedures and instruments for real agreement in macro-economic policies that is also compatible with the accords included in the stability pact," he said.
The stability pact, agreed last year in Dublin, aims to ensure the stability of European post-EMU economic conditions.
Delors said such a commitment would help smooth out possible shocks within the European economy, while promoting growth and job creation.

He added that the laws and statutes relating to the German Bundesbank -- which among other things listed its goals as including price stability, full employment and sufficient growth -- showed that such a move was not necessarily incompatible with central bank independence.
"The same (goals) will apply to the European Central Bank, whose independence will naturally be completely respected," Delors, European Commission president between 1985-95, said.
